messages.subject: Testing group difference across two parameters in model
parts:
Dear all,

I was hoping I could get some help with checking that the following logic is ok: I want to test whether two groups differ across two parameters of my learning model (like an ANOVA across these parameters). The parameters measure how much their learning is interfered by two different external factors (that's why I called them 'InterF1' and 'InterF2' here). The code is attached. The main part of interest is in the transformed data block where I'm trying to sample each person's InterF1, InterF2:

transformed parameters{
  for (s in 1:15){ // Drug group
    InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
    InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
  for (s in 16:nsub){ // Placebo group
    InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
    InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
}

The model runs very slowly, compared to a model where I just sample InterF1 and InterF2 directly (from e.g. for drug group: InterF1[drug] ~ normal(mu_InterF1drug, sd_InterF1). But the number of samples for the mu_InterfGroupDiff is very high (~ number of samples drawn), so maybe this is not too bad. Is there anyway to code this better?

I'm also not sure whether if I wanted to model the standard deviation also as different between the groups, I could just replace for example sd_InterF1 with something like sd_InterF1Drug and sd_InterF1Placebo?

The last part I'm not quite sure about is how I can limit the parameters - I would expect InterF1 and InterF2 to be between -1 and +1. This is also ok for the group level parameters that I can limit as I want. But if I try to limit InterF1, the model produces problems because the sums can fall outside this interval.

Many thanks
Jacquie

Full example code:
parameters{
  // group level
  real mu_alpha_pr;
  real mu_beta_pr;
  real<lower=-1,upper=1> mu_InterfGeneral;   // how much a person is interfered on average across the two measures
  real<lower=-1,upper=1> mu_InterfGroupDiff; // group difference between drug and placebo
  real<lower=-1,upper=1> mu_InterfType;      // how much Interference factor 1 and Interference factor 2 differ for each person

  real <lower=0> sd_alpha;
  real <lower=0> sd_beta;
  real <lower=0> sd_InterF1;
  real <lower=0> sd_InterF2;

  // Individual subjects
  real alpha_pr[nsub];
  real beta_pr[nsub];
  real InterF1_pr[nsub];
  real InterF2_pr[nsub];
}
transformed parameters{
  real mu_alpha;
  real mu_beta;

  real<lower=0,upper=1>  alpha;
  real<lower=0,upper=10> beta;
  real<lower=-5,upper=5> InterF1;
  real<lower=-5,upper=5> InterF2;

  mu_alpha    <- Phi(mu_alpha_pr);
  mu_beta     <- Phi(mu_beta_pr)*10;

  for (s in 1:15){ // Drug group
    alpha[s]      <- Phi(alpha_pr[s]);
    beta[s]       <- Phi(beta_pr[s])*10;
    InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
    InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
  for (s in 16:nsub){ // Placebo group
    alpha[s]      <- Phi(alpha_pr[s]);
    beta[s]       <- Phi(beta_pr[s])*10;
    InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
    InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
}

model{
  // Draw parameters
  mu_alpha_pr ~ normal(0,1);
  mu_beta_pr  ~ normal(0,1);
  mu_InterfGeneral   ~ normal(0,1);
  mu_InterfGroupDiff ~ normal(0,1);
  mu_InterfType      ~ normal(0,1);

  sd_alpha   ~ normal(0,1000);
  sd_beta    ~ normal(0,1000);
  sd_InterF1 ~ normal(0,1000);
  sd_InterF2 ~ normal(0,1000);

  InterF1_pr ~ normal(0,1);
  InterF2_pr ~ normal(0,1);
  
  // Do the learning (shortened)
  for (s in 1:nsub){
    for (t in 1:ntrials)
      for (o in 1:2){
        Prediction[s,t+1,o] <- (alpha[s]- InterF1[s]*Dat1 - InterF2[s]*Dat2) * (Prediction[s,t,o]-Outcome[s,t,o]);
      }
      DecisionPred[s,t] <- 1.0/(1.0+exp(beta[s]*(Predictions[s,t,2]-Predictions[s,t,1])))
    }
  }
}

> But the problem with this is that I'm not sure how to code 'NOISE'

You want to think about modeling the noise probabilistically,
then the formulation becomes easy. Think about the usual formulation
of regression:

y = beta * x + epsilon
epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma)

To write this out in Stan, you have:

y ~ normal(beta * x, sigma);

There's no explicit representation of epsilon. Now you
could equivalently, but much more confusingly, write:

real epsilon;
epsilon <- y - beta * x;
epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma);

You just need to do the same thing for your problem (only
you need to scale epsilon).

- Bob

The idea is that you want:

You can make a variable out of prediction error. I'll keep going
back to the simple regression case, which shows the difference:

This is:

y[n] = x[n] * beta + epsilon[n]
epsilon ~ normal(0, 1)

transformed parameters {
vector[N] epsilon;
for (n in 1:N)
epsilon[n] <- y[n] - x[n] * beta;
}
model {
epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma);

Here's the way to do it without epsilon being saved:

model {
vector[N] epsilon;
for (n in 1:N)
epsilon[n] <- y[n] - x[n] * beta;

epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma);

model {
y[n] ~ normal(x[n] * beta, sigma);

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Testing group difference across two parameters in model
parts:
Stan gripes if you don't formulate your model in typical
generative terms.

You'll have to post the rest of your Stan program for us
to see what's going on; the real problem in your fragment
is that you never define y[n].

- Bob

> On Mar 7, 2016, at 5:29 AM, Jacqueline Scholl <jacqueli...@psy.ox.ac.uk> wrote:
>
> I see, so I have now:
> data{
> dat [N];}
>
> model{
> real y[N];
>
> for (n in 1:N)
> y[n] ~ normal(RPE,sigma)
> dat[n]~ bernoulli(f(y)); //with the function f doing a softmax transform of y as typical for a learning/decision model
> }
>
> but now stan says 'Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
> compile: If so, you need to call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.' (for the line where I sample y[n])
>
> I think the problem is that I'm trying to say that there is noise for the learning process (y[n]~...) and the decision (dat[n]~...) ?
> Sorry that I'm a bit slow at understanding this..
>
> On Mon, Mar 7, 2016 at 5:38 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> You can make a variable out of prediction error. I'll keep going
> back to the simple regression case, which shows the difference:
>
> This is:
>
> y[n] = x[n] * beta + epsilon[n]
> epsilon ~ normal(0, 1)
>
> transformed parameters {
> vector[N] epsilon;
> for (n in 1:N)
> epsilon[n] <- y[n] - x[n] * beta;
> }
> model {
> epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma);
>
> Here's the way to do it without epsilon being saved:
>
> model {
> vector[N] epsilon;
> for (n in 1:N)
> epsilon[n] <- y[n] - x[n] * beta;
>
> epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma);
>
> And here's the way to do it without an explicit epsilon:
>
> model {
> y[n] ~ normal(x[n] * beta, sigma);
>
> It works out to the same density either way.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>

> > yes, that's pretty much what I'm trying to do;

> >
> > The idea is that you want:

> >
> > where f( ) is some update function to predict the new observation

parts:
And when I say "define" I mean define. You declare it
as a real N-array, but then you use it in the ~ statement
before it's defined. The ~ doesn't do a random draw; it's
just shorthand to increment the log density.

- Bob

> On Mar 7, 2016, at 5:29 AM, Jacqueline Scholl <jacqueli...@psy.ox.ac.uk> wrote:
>
> I see, so I have now:
> data{
> dat [N];}
>
> model{
> real y[N];
>
> for (n in 1:N)
> y[n] ~ normal(RPE,sigma)
> dat[n]~ bernoulli(f(y)); //with the function f doing a softmax transform of y as typical for a learning/decision model
> }
>
> but now stan says 'Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
> compile: If so, you need to call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.' (for the line where I sample y[n])
>
> I think the problem is that I'm trying to say that there is noise for the learning process (y[n]~...) and the decision (dat[n]~...) ?
> Sorry that I'm a bit slow at understanding this..
>
> On Mon, Mar 7, 2016 at 5:38 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> You can make a variable out of prediction error. I'll keep going
> back to the simple regression case, which shows the difference:
>
> This is:
>
> y[n] = x[n] * beta + epsilon[n]
> epsilon ~ normal(0, 1)
>
> transformed parameters {
> vector[N] epsilon;
> for (n in 1:N)
> epsilon[n] <- y[n] - x[n] * beta;
> }
> model {
> epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma);
>
> Here's the way to do it without epsilon being saved:
>
> model {
> vector[N] epsilon;
> for (n in 1:N)
> epsilon[n] <- y[n] - x[n] * beta;
>
> epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma);
>
> And here's the way to do it without an explicit epsilon:
>
> model {
> y[n] ~ normal(x[n] * beta, sigma);
>
> It works out to the same density either way.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
> > On Mar 6, 2016, at 10:50 AM, Jacqueline Scholl <jacqueli...@psy.ox.ac.uk> wrote:
> >
> > yes, that's pretty much what I'm trying to do;
> >
> > I'm trying to code a variant of a reinforcement learning model. In this kind of model, there is usually no noise in the learning steps, but only 'noise' when the learnt information gets transformed into a binary choice between e.g. two options the participant selects between based on the learnt information.
> >
> > The standard learning model is something like this:
> > (for each participant and trial t)
> > PredictionError[t]<- Outcome[t]-Prediction[t]; // Outcome would here be say 1 or 0 for getting a reward or not getting one and prediction is how likely the participant/ model thinks the option is going to have a reward
> > Prediction[t+1] <- Prediction[t] + LearningRate[p]*PredictionError[t]; // The Prediction error is used to update the prediction (where the learning rate determines how much the prediction error is weighted
> > RealChoice[t]~bernoulli(f(Predictions[t]); // the predictions for the two option to determine which choice participants are likely to make, and then compare that to the Real choice.
> >
> > What I want to capture now is that there might also be some noise in the learning process itself (for example, my neural data suggests to me that a drug improves the representation of the prediction error in one group). How can I capture this noise?
> > I've tried to add it to the prediction error:
> > PredictionErrorTemp[t] <- Outcome[t]-Prediction[t]; //as before
> > PredictionError[t] ~ normal(PredictionErrorTemp[t],noise[p]); // where noise[s] says how much each participant is representation is noisy.
> > rest as before.
> >
> > The problem now is that I have so far tried to sample PredictionError (or rather the 'Matt trick transform' of it) as a parameter because if I write the code as an _lp function, I can't use it in the generated quantities block. But having this as a parameter (i.e. having as many values as participants x trials) does not seem right either.
> >
> > On Fri, Mar 4, 2016 at 11:45 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > I'd need to see more of what you're trying to do. Can you
> > write the density down in math terms without worrying about
> > coding in Stan?
> >
> > The idea is that you want:
> >
> > y[t + 1] ~ normal(f(y[t],theta), noise);
> >
> > where f( ) is some update function to predict the new observation
> > at time t+1 based on the previous observation at t and some parameters theta.
> > Then the function isn't exact and gets some noise.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> >
> > > On Mar 4, 2016, at 4:50 AM, Jacqueline Scholl <jacqueli...@psy.ox.ac.uk> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi Bob,
> > >
> > > thanks for your help.
> > > So basically, if I understand you right, you're suggesting:
> > > PredictErrorOld <- Oucome-Prediction
> > > PredictErrorNew ~ normal(PredictErrorOld,sigma)
> > > and then sigma (with an individual value for each person, constraint by a group normal) is a measure of the noise as in standard deviation of the distribution.
> > >
> > > Silly question now, would I code PredictErrorNew as a parameter? Because then the problem is that Stan is fitting this on a trial-by-trial basis (which is maybe why it doesn't converge even after 10,000 iterations). When I tried to just have PredictErrorNew as a variable in the function block, I can't call the function (with '_lp' in the end) from the generated quantities block.
> > >
> > > I'm wondering whether it's maybe a problem with the steps that happen with the PredictErrorNew quantity after I make it:
> > > - Use it to update the predicted reward value (this is a learning model)
> > > - Use the predicted reward value to compute the choice probability
> > > - Link that to the real choice with RealChoice ~ bernoulli(PredictedChoice) [this one is only in the model block, not in the generated quantities block, where I instead use the PredictedChoice to compute the log likelihood]
> > >
> > > [I think that with the 'Matt trick', this may transform to my original:
> > > PredictErrorNew_raw <-normal(0,1) (what I called 'NOISE')
> > > PredictErrorNew <- PredictErrorOld + sigma*PredictErrorNew_raw (where .._raw is 'NOISE' and sigma is 'InterF1')
> > > ]
> > >
> > > On Thu, Mar 3, 2016 at 8:31 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > On Mar 3, 2016, at 1:05 PM, jacquie...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > >
> > > > I've been thinking that maybe it would actually be more accurate to model this interference as adding some noise to the representation of the prediction error (Outcome[s,t,o]-Prediction[s,t,o]).
> > > >
> > > > I've tried to do this as:
> > > > Prediction[s,t+1,o] <- alpha[s]*(Outcome[s,t,o]-Prediction[s,t,o]+NOISE*InterF1[s]);
> > > >
> > >
> > > > But the problem with this is that I'm not sure how to code 'NOISE'
> > >
> > > You want to think about modeling the noise probabilistically,
> > > then the formulation becomes easy. Think about the usual formulation
> > > of regression:
> > >
> > > y = beta * x + epsilon
> > > epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma)
> > >
> > > To write this out in Stan, you have:
> > >
> > > y ~ normal(beta * x, sigma);
> > >
> > > There's no explicit representation of epsilon. Now you
> > > could equivalently, but much more confusingly, write:
> > >
> > > real epsilon;
> > > epsilon <- y - beta * x;
> > > epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma);
> > >
> > > You just need to do the same thing for your problem (only
> > > you need to scale epsilon).
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > - I have tried:
> > > > for (s in 1:nsub){
> > > > for (t in 1:ntrials){
> > > > for (o in 1:2){
> > > > NOISE[s,t,o] ~ normal(0,1);
> > > > }}}
> > > > but if I then have 'NOISE' in the parameter block (as otherwise, stan tells me that I can't use my model in the generated quantities block by calling a function), the model then fits some value for NOISE on each trial. This seems wrong?
> > > >
> > > > On Monday, February 29, 2016 at 3:05:57 PM UTC, jacquie...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Dear all,
> > > >
> > > > I was hoping I could get some help with checking that the following logic is ok: I want to test whether two groups differ across two parameters of my learning model (like an ANOVA across these parameters). The parameters measure how much their learning is interfered by two different external factors (that's why I called them 'InterF1' and 'InterF2' here). The code is attached. The main part of interest is in the transformed data block where I'm trying to sample each person's InterF1, InterF2:
> > > >
> > > > transformed parameters{
> > > > for (s in 1:15){ // Drug group
> > > > InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
> > > > InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
> > > > for (s in 16:nsub){ // Placebo group
> > > > InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
> > > > InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > The model runs very slowly, compared to a model where I just sample InterF1 and InterF2 directly (from e.g. for drug group: InterF1[drug] ~ normal(mu_InterF1drug, sd_InterF1). But the number of samples for the mu_InterfGroupDiff is very high (~ number of samples drawn), so maybe this is not too bad. Is there anyway to code this better?
> > > >
> > > > I'm also not sure whether if I wanted to model the standard deviation also as different between the groups, I could just replace for example sd_InterF1 with something like sd_InterF1Drug and sd_InterF1Placebo?
> > > >
> > > > The last part I'm not quite sure about is how I can limit the parameters - I would expect InterF1 and InterF2 to be between -1 and +1. This is also ok for the group level parameters that I can limit as I want. But if I try to limit InterF1, the model produces problems because the sums can fall outside this interval.
> > > >
> > > > Many thanks
> > > > Jacquie
> > > >
> > > > Full example code:
> > > > parameters{
> > > > // group level
> > > > real mu_alpha_pr;
> > > > real mu_beta_pr;
> > > > real<lower=-1,upper=1> mu_InterfGeneral; // how much a person is interfered on average across the two measures
> > > > real<lower=-1,upper=1> mu_InterfGroupDiff; // group difference between drug and placebo
> > > > real<lower=-1,upper=1> mu_InterfType; // how much Interference factor 1 and Interference factor 2 differ for each person
> > > >
> > > > real <lower=0> sd_alpha;
> > > > real <lower=0> sd_beta;
> > > > real <lower=0> sd_InterF1;
> > > > real <lower=0> sd_InterF2;
> > > >
> > > > // Individual subjects
> > > > real alpha_pr[nsub];
> > > > real beta_pr[nsub];
> > > > real InterF1_pr[nsub];
> > > > real InterF2_pr[nsub];
> > > > }
> > > > transformed parameters{
> > > > real mu_alpha;
> > > > real mu_beta;
> > > >
> > > > real<lower=0,upper=1> alpha;
> > > > real<lower=0,upper=10> beta;
> > > > real<lower=-5,upper=5> InterF1;
> > > > real<lower=-5,upper=5> InterF2;
> > > >
> > > > mu_alpha <- Phi(mu_alpha_pr);
> > > > mu_beta <- Phi(mu_beta_pr)*10;
> > > >
> > > > for (s in 1:15){ // Drug group
> > > > alpha[s] <- Phi(alpha_pr[s]);
> > > > beta[s] <- Phi(beta_pr[s])*10;
> > > > InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
> > > > InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
> > > > for (s in 16:nsub){ // Placebo group
> > > > alpha[s] <- Phi(alpha_pr[s]);
> > > > beta[s] <- Phi(beta_pr[s])*10;
> > > > InterF1[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff + 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF1*InterF1_pr[s];
> > > > InterF2[nsub] <- (mu_InterfGeneral - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfGroupDiff - 1.0/2.0*mu_InterfType) + sd_InterF2*InterF2_pr[s];}
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > model{
> > > > // Draw parameters
> > > > mu_alpha_pr ~ normal(0,1);
> > > > mu_beta_pr ~ normal(0,1);
> > > > mu_InterfGeneral ~ normal(0,1);
> > > > mu_InterfGroupDiff ~ normal(0,1);
> > > > mu_InterfType ~ normal(0,1);
> > > >
> > > > sd_alpha ~ normal(0,1000);
> > > > sd_beta ~ normal(0,1000);
> > > > sd_InterF1 ~ normal(0,1000);
> > > > sd_InterF2 ~ normal(0,1000);
> > > >
> > > > InterF1_pr ~ normal(0,1);
> > > > InterF2_pr ~ normal(0,1);
> > > >
> > > > // Do the learning (shortened)
> > > > for (s in 1:nsub){
> > > > for (t in 1:ntrials)
> > > > for (o in 1:2){
> > > > Prediction[s,t+1,o] <- (alpha[s]- InterF1[s]*Dat1 - InterF2[s]*Dat2) * (Prediction[s,t,o]-Outcome[s,t,o]);
> > > > }
> > > > DecisionPred[s,t] <- 1.0/(1.0+exp(beta[s]*(Predictions[s,t,2]-Predictions[s,t,1])))
> > > > }
> > > > }
> > > > }
